title: Line is not a record
why: Every Intel HEX line must begin with ':' and every Motorola line with 'S'. Anything else is a paste artefact, a diff marker or a stray editor line, and most programmers stop at it.

title: Non-hex or odd-length record
why: A record is whole bytes of uppercase-or-lowercase hex. An odd digit count or a stray character means a byte was dropped or split when the file was edited or generated.

title: Byte-count field disagrees with the data
why: The LL field states how many data bytes follow. When a patch adds or removes bytes without fixing LL, loaders read past the end of the record or truncate it silently.

title: Intel HEX checksum is wrong
why: The last byte is the two's complement of the sum of every byte before it. Hand-edited and machine-patched records almost always leave the old checksum behind; strict programmers abort, lax ones flash the record anyway.

title: Unknown Intel HEX record type
why: Only types 00-05 are defined. An unknown type is a corrupted address field or a file from a different format, and behaviour is undefined across toolchains.

title: Missing or malformed end-of-file record
why: An Intel HEX image must end with :00000001FF. Without it a programmer cannot tell a complete image from a truncated download, and some simply hang waiting for more.

title: Records after the end-of-file record
why: Everything after the EOF record is ignored by conforming loaders. Appending a patch to the end of a .hex file is the classic way to ship a fix that never reaches the device.

title: Two records write the same address
why: When two data records cover the same absolute byte, the flashed value depends on the load order of the tool. Merged images and appended patches are where this comes from.

title: Address wraps past 64 KiB with no extended-address record
why: Type 00 records carry only 16 address bits. Past 0xFFFF an image needs a type 04 or type 02 record; without one the data lands back at the bottom of memory.

title: S-record checksum is wrong
why: An S-record checksum is 0xFF minus the sum of the count, address and data bytes. A wrong one means the line was edited after generation.

title: S-record count field or terminator is wrong
why: The count byte covers address + data + checksum, and an S-record image must end with S7, S8 or S9. A wrong count shifts the checksum byte; a missing terminator leaves the entry point undefined.

title: S5/S6 record tally does not match
why: S5 and S6 declare how many data records the file contains. A tally that no longer matches is proof the file was cut, merged or filtered after it was built.

title: Unwritten gap inside the image
why: A gap means those cells keep whatever was in flash before. If the gap is not deliberate erased space it is a section the linker placed and the image dropped.

title: Block does not sit on a flash page boundary
why: Page-programmed flash writes whole pages. A block that starts or ends mid-page forces a read-modify-write, and on parts without it the rest of the page is erased.

title: Start address is outside the written image
why: A type 03/05 or S7/S8/S9 record names the entry point. If it points at an address the image never writes, the device jumps into unprogrammed flash.

title: Mixed-case hex digits
why: The format allows either case, but a file that switches case mid-way is a file that two different tools have written, which is worth knowing before you trust its checksums.
